sections.h2: What are the ways to sell a house in St. Louis, MO?
sections.html:
Owners in St. Louis can hire an agent, go it alone, or take an investor's cash bid on the property in its present condition. All three routes meet the same city requirement: a Housing Conservation inspection that yields a Certificate of Inspection before the next household moves in.

The trade-off is mostly time against price. Putting the house on the market can reach more buyers, but you will clean, stage and wait out showings and a buyer's lender. A direct sale to an investor can close on a date you choose, which matters when you are inheriting a house in another state, carrying a vacant building, or sorting out a tenant situation.

  • Listing: the widest buyer pool and the longest timeline, with costs set in your listing agreement.
  • Selling by owner: you handle pricing, showings and paperwork, and a title company or attorney still has to close it.
  • Cash bid: fewer showings and a quicker closing, at a price that reflects the repairs the buyer takes on.

sections.h2: What kind of city is St. Louis for a home seller?
sections.html:
St. Louis is an independent city, meaning it sits outside St. Louis County. According to Wikipedia, it separated from the county in 1877, and it is divided into 79 officially recognized neighborhoods. That split matters for sellers: city ordinances, the city Recorder of Deeds and the city Collector of Revenue apply to a house inside the limits, while a house a few blocks west across the boundary falls under county and municipal rules instead.

Census estimates put the city at 278,144 residents in mid-2025, a drop of 7.7% from the April 2020 base. Only 45.3% of housing units are owner-occupied, so a large share of the stock is rented, and many sellers here are landlords or heirs rather than owner-occupants. Brick is a defining material: the city's older districts include Laclede's Landing, with its cobblestone streets and brick and cast-iron warehouses, and Lafayette Square, where many houses blend Greek Revival, Federal and Italianate styles.

Distinct communities shape demand block by block. Dutchtown, Cherokee Street in Benton Park West, and The Hill each have their own character, while the Central West End sits beside the Washington University medical campus and the Cortex innovation district.

sections.h2: What does a St. Louis occupancy inspection involve when a house sells?
sections.html:
When an occupied house sells in St. Louis and no Certificate of Inspection has been issued in the last 12 months, the sale triggers a new one. City Building Division materials state that 100% of the city lies inside a Housing Conservation District under Ordinance No. 71835, so the requirement applies citywide.

The inspection is a basic code check of the interior and exterior under the International Property Maintenance Code. It is not a warranty of the building, and the city itself suggests that buyers consider a commercial grade inspection. Details sellers should know:

  • The application costs $120.00, or $200.00 if someone is found living in the dwelling without a current certificate.
  • The inspection can be scheduled no sooner than 3 business days and no later than 15 days after applying.
  • Water and electric must be on at the time of the visit.
  • If the certificate is issued with violations, the owner has 30 days to make repairs, and extensions may be granted for weather or other specific causes.
  • A certificate is valid for 12 months, and the inspection also sets the number of people who may occupy the unit. No more than three unrelated persons may live in one dwelling.

Apply online through the city's permit portal or in person at City Hall, 1200 Market Street, Room 425. Call the Building Division at (314) 622-3313 with questions about a particular address.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about housing in St. Louis?
sections.html:
The 2020 to 2024 survey figures describe a city with lower home values than the suburbs to its northwest. Its median owner-occupied value of $197,500 trails St. Charles at $298,700 and St. Peters at $269,900.

sections.h2: Where are St. Louis deeds recorded, and what should a seller expect?
sections.html:
Deeds for property in the city are recorded with the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, in City Hall at 1200 Market Street, Room 126. Counter hours are weekdays, 8:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m., and the land records line is (314) 622-3260. The department also offers a free online search of recorded land documents, which lets you confirm that your own deed, any old mortgage and any lien show up the way you expect before you sign a contract.

Missouri law lets spouses convey real estate by joint deed (RSMo 442.030). If the property is held as tenants by the entirety, both spouses are bound by the covenants in the deed, so both need to sign. Heirs selling an inherited house should ask the title company which probate papers it needs to see.

On the tax side, ask the St. Louis Collector of Revenue what is currently owed on your parcel before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: How do weather and the ground affect a St. Louis house?
sections.html:
Summers here run hot and sticky while winters turn cold. At Lambert airport the 1991 to 2020 normals show about 41.70 inches of precipitation and 16.6 inches of snow a year, and the area sees thunderstorms on about 48 days annually. Wikipedia notes that severe storms, hail and tornadoes are possible in spring, and that the Great Flood of 1993 is part of the region's record.

For a seller, that means buyers and inspectors look hard at roofs, gutters, chimneys and basements. The same source notes that the area south of downtown has numerous sinkholes and caves, though most caves in the city have been sealed. A cash buyer prices these conditions in directly, while a financed buyer may ask for repairs after their own inspection.

sections.h2: What steps should a St. Louis seller take first?
sections.html:
Start with paperwork, then decide how much repair work is worth doing.

  • Pull your deed and any payoff statements, and check them against the Recorder of Deeds online search.
  • Find out whether a Certificate of Inspection was issued in the last 12 months. If so, you may not need a new one.
  • Walk the house for exterior violations under the property maintenance code, since the city checks the exterior as well as the interior.
  • Confirm water and electric will be on for inspection day.
  • Compare a listing estimate, a by-owner plan and a cash offer on the amount you would actually keep.

If the house is vacant, damaged or tenant-occupied, a cash sale as-is can remove several of these steps, though the buyer still needs the Certificate of Inspection before anyone occupies the unit.

faqs.q: Is an inspection required before a St. Louis house changes hands?
faqs.a: Yes, for an occupied house. The city requires a Certificate of Inspection when an occupied structure sells and none has been issued in the last 12 months. The application is $120.00, or $200.00 if the home is occupied without a current certificate.

faqs.q: How long does a St. Louis Certificate of Inspection last?
faqs.a: It is valid for 12 months. If violations are noted when it is issued, the owner has 30 days to fix them, with extensions possible for weather or other specific causes.

faqs.q: Can I sell a St. Louis house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. You can list it, sell it by owner, or sell it as-is to a cash buyer. The inspection is a basic code check, not a full condition report, and the occupancy certificate is required before anyone moves in.

faqs.q: Where do I record the deed after a St. Louis sale?
faqs.a: At the City of St. Louis Recorder of Deeds, Land Records Department, City Hall Room 126, 1200 Market Street. The phone number is (314) 622-3260, and your title company normally handles the filing at closing.

faqs.q: How many unrelated people can live in a St. Louis dwelling?
faqs.a: No more than three. The Housing Conservation inspection also sets the number of people who may safely occupy the unit, which matters for rental properties being sold.
